# AppInspect

> AppInspect is a free Android library that adds a full-screen inspector to a host
> app's own debug and internal builds. It captures OkHttp traffic, can replace any
> API response with a mock, and shows SharedPreferences, DataStore, SQLite/Room,
> WorkManager jobs, crashes and ANRs, a live logcat tail, and runtime metadata — all
> on the device, with no proxy, no USB cable, no account and no telemetry. Everything
> is on by default and no configuration is required. A no-op artifact keeps the
> inspection code out of release APKs.

- Artifact group: `io.github.appinspect`
- Published on: Maven Central
- Version: this documentation tracks the latest published release; check Maven Central for the current version number
- Minimum Android version: 7.0 (API 24). ANR and native crash reporting need Android 11 (API 30).
- License cost: free
- Website: https://app-inspect-doc.vercel.app/
- Sample app (runnable Android project with the library wired in): https://github.com/appinspect/AppInspect-Sample-App
- Maintainer: Suryansh Prajapati
- Content last updated: 2026-09-01
- This file is canonical. Every claim below is also stated on the linked page, and the
  pages are the source of truth if the two ever disagree.

## In one sentence

AppInspect is a free Android library you add to your own app's debug and QA builds to
see, on the device and without a laptop, what the app is actually doing: its API calls,
its stored data, its background jobs, its crashes, and its log output.

## Installation

```kotlin
dependencies {
    debugImplementation("io.github.appinspect:appinspect:<latest-version>")
    releaseImplementation("io.github.appinspect:appinspect-no-op:<latest-version>")
}
```

AppInspect auto-initialises through AndroidX Startup, so no `Application` class change
is required and every feature — panels, shake, launcher shortcut, crash capture,
notifications, logcat — is on by default. To change something, prefer
`AppInspect.updateConfiguration { … }`, which keeps the build-tier enablement AppInspect
inferred; `AppInspect.install(application, configuration)` replaces the configuration
wholesale and discards that inference, including a staging variant's resource opt-in.

## Sample app

A runnable demonstration project lives at
https://github.com/appinspect/AppInspect-Sample-App — a small Kotlin app whose only
purpose is to show the library working. Clone it, run the debug variant
(`./gradlew :app:installDebug`), generate some data from the on-screen buttons, then open
the inspector. It is also the shortest integration reference: the whole wiring is the two
dependency lines in `app/build.gradle.kts`, `addAppInspectInterceptor()` on the OkHttp
builder, and a debug-only object holding the `open()` / `updateConfiguration()` calls that
the no-op artifact does not contain. The clone command is on
https://app-inspect-doc.vercel.app/install.html#sample-app.

## Builds and environments

AppInspect never sees Gradle variant names. It resolves a build to one of three tiers
from two inputs: `FLAG_DEBUGGABLE` (from the build type's `isDebuggable`), and the
boolean resource `appinspect_enabled_in_non_debuggable_build`.

- debuggable → `DEBUG` tier, everything enabled, nothing to configure.
- not debuggable + resource `true` → `STAGING` tier, everything enabled.
- not debuggable + resource `false`/absent (the default) → `PRODUCTION` tier, everything
  disabled. The safe outcome is the one you get by doing nothing.

A custom variant (`staging`, `uat`, `qa`, `internalTest`, …) that sets
`isDebuggable = true` needs no further work. A non-debuggable one opts in with one line —
`resValue("bool", "appinspect_enabled_in_non_debuggable_build", "true")` in the build
type, or the same boolean in `src/<variant>/res/values/` — plus `matchingFallbacks`,
which any custom build type needs because AppInspect publishes only `debug` and
`release` variants. `appinspect_environment_name` optionally labels the environment in
the Runtime panel. The opt-in is a resource rather than an API call for two reasons:
AppInspect installs itself from AndroidX Startup before `Application.onCreate()`, and
Android never merges one variant's resources into another, so the value is physically
absent from the release APK.

Minification, R8 and resource shrinking need no host configuration: AppInspect ships its
own `consumerProguardFiles`. Writing the opt-in resource into the `release` build type or
`src/main/res/` while the full library is on the release classpath *will* run the
inspector in production; keeping `releaseImplementation(appinspect-no-op)` makes that
unreachable.

## Host compatibility

minSdk 24, AndroidX required. Compose is **not** required in the host app (the inspector's
Compose UI is already compiled into the published AAR); Kotlin is not required either, and
Java-only hosts call `AppInspect.INSTANCE.…` and add the two interceptors directly. No DI
framework, no `Application` subclass, no manifest changes and no permissions to declare.
OkHttp, WorkManager and `androidx.security-crypto` are `compileOnly`, so AppInspect never
forces a version onto the host app — which matters because raising the host's OkHttp
version would mean the tested build runs a different HTTP stack than release. Missing
integrations degrade to an empty or opaque panel rather than failing. By API level:
launcher shortcut needs 25, notification channels 26, ANR/native crash detection 30,
and the `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` runtime grant 33.

Network capture is opt-in and requires one line on the OkHttp builder, added last:

```kotlin
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addAppInspectInterceptor()   // last
    .build()
```

Last matters for two reasons: a `SHORT_CIRCUIT` mock skips every interceptor
registered after AppInspect's, and last is where the request looks the way it goes
out. The extension also installs a network-level interceptor so recorded events carry
the final wire request headers, including an `Authorization` header added downstream.

The rule is generic, not per-library: **if OkHttp is the engine underneath, AppInspect can
capture it** — whatever sits on top. Two shapes cover almost everything:

- **The library takes a client you built** — Retrofit, Apollo, Coil. Instrument the builder
  above and hand it over: `Retrofit.Builder().client(instrumentedClient)`.
- **The library builds its own and exposes the builder** — Ktor on the `OkHttp` engine
  (`io.ktor:ktor-client-okhttp`), whose `engine { config { … } }` block takes an
  `OkHttpClient.Builder.() -> Unit`.

Not backed by OkHttp — Volley, Cronet, `HttpURLConnection`, a WebView, Ktor on a non-OkHttp
engine — means nothing to hook: Network and Mocks stay empty, every other panel is unaffected.

```kotlin
val client = HttpClient(OkHttp) {
    engine {
        addInterceptor(authInterceptor)
        config { addAppInspectInterceptor() }   // last
    }
}
```

Ktor specifics:

- Ordering inside `engine { }` is preserved (`addInterceptor`, `addNetworkInterceptor` and
  `config { }` all append to the same builder), so last still means last.
- `engine { preconfigured = instrumentedClient }` is an equivalent route.
- Mocking works — a mock is served from inside OkHttp, so Ktor never sees the difference.
- `CIO`, `Android`, `Java` and `Darwin` expose no interceptor and capture nothing.
- The OkHttp engine disables OkHttp's own redirect following and lets Ktor's `HttpRedirect`
  plugin handle hops, so a redirect chain is one captured event per hop — as is each
  `HttpRequestRetry` attempt.
- Streaming and `MultiPartFormDataContent` uploads arrive as one-shot OkHttp bodies that
  AppInspect will not drain, so those events record everything except the request body.
  Byte-backed bodies — JSON via `ContentNegotiation`, form content, plain text — are captured
  normally, and response bodies are never affected on any engine.

`AppInspect.install()`, `AppInspect.open()` and the long-press trigger helpers do not
exist in `appinspect-no-op`, so keep those calls in a debug-only source set. The
interceptor line is designed to compile in every variant.

## Opening the inspector

Shake gesture (`shakeToOpenEnabled`, default threshold 2.7 g total accelerometer
magnitude), launcher shortcut (`launcherShortcutEnabled`), long press on a View
(`AppInspect.attachLongPressTrigger`) or a composable
(`Modifier.appInspectLongPressTrigger`), tapping a network notification, or
`AppInspect.open(context)`. By default the inspector opens in its own task, so it gets
a separate Recents card and supports split-screen, while still running in the host
process.

## Panels

Five bottom-bar panels — Network, Mocks, Storage, Work, Crashes — navigated by tap or
swipe. Runtime and Logcat are top-bar buttons rather than tabs. Any panel can open a
large value in a shared full-screen JSON tree viewer.

- Network: filters and search across endpoints, headers, bodies and cURL; wire request
  headers; JSON/XML formatting; long-press quick actions; export as `.txt` (with cURL)
  or `.har` (HAR 1.2); live notifications; default retention 300 events.
- Mocks: replace a live response. Rules come from `assets/appinspect/mocks.json` or
  from the panel; runtime rules win. `SHORT_CIRCUIT` never touches the network,
  `OVERRIDE` lets the real call complete then replaces status/headers/body and keeps
  the original status in `X-AppInspect-Mock-Original-Status`. Matching on method, URL
  substring with `*` wildcards, query parameters and a request-body substring — all
  filters on the outgoing request, which is never modified. Also artificial delay and
  `IO_EXCEPTION` / `SOCKET_TIMEOUT` failure simulation. First match wins, ordered by
  runtime priority then bundled priority. Mocking requires five gates to pass: build
  tier, `allowResponseMocking`, the tri-state device switch, `"mockingEnabled"` in the
  file, and the rule's own `enabled` flag.
- Storage: SharedPreferences (read and write, with read-only decrypted
  `EncryptedSharedPreferences`), Jetpack DataStore (read only, custom protobuf
  parser), SQLite and Room (schema, paged rows, structured editing, optional SQL
  console). Search is debounced and runs off the main thread.
- WorkManager: every persisted work spec from the app and any library, with state,
  constraints, attempts, backoff, input/output/progress data, last stop reason
  (WorkManager 2.9+) and periodic/expedited details. Read only by design.
- Crashes and ANRs: uncaught exceptions captured on all threads and written
  synchronously before the process dies, chaining to any existing handler such as
  Crashlytics; ANRs and native crashes read from `ApplicationExitInfo` on Android 11+
  and reported on the next launch, including the OS ANR thread dump. 50 most recent
  records persist.
- Runtime: app, environment, device and session metadata, plus host-supplied custom
  metadata.
- Logcat: a live terminal tail of the app's own log output — every `Log.*` call from the
  host and from any library in the same process. Level/tag/text/regex filters with inline
  highlighting, pause, follow-tail, expandable folded stack traces, wrap and redact
  toggles, and a `.txt` share of the visible lines. No permission is needed (capture is
  constrained to the app's own pid, the only log Android lets an app read), nothing is
  written to disk (a bounded in-memory ring buffer, 2,000 entries by default), and there
  is no idle cost (no thread and no `logcat` process until the page is opened). Scroll-back
  comes from replaying Android's own log buffer on open.
- Value viewer: JSON tree with collapse/expand, child counts, line-number gutter,
  auto-detected escaped JSON strings opened as real subtrees, raw view, and content
  search that stays responsive on multi-hundred-kilobyte payloads.

## Configuration

`AppInspectConfiguration` groups: `enablement`, `entryPoints`, `panels`, `powerTools`,
`logs`, `retention`, `environment`, `initialMetadata`, `redaction`, `branding`.

- `enablement`: `allowedBuildTiers` (debug only by default), `allowInNonDebugBuilds`,
  `allowInProductionBuilds`. Production requires both flags shipped as true in the APK.
  `setEnabled(...)` is ANDed with the tier check, so it can turn an enabled build off but
  can never turn a disallowed tier on.
- `entryPoints`: `shakeToOpenEnabled`, `shakeThresholdGravity`, `shakeCooldownMillis`,
  `launcherShortcutEnabled`, `autoOpenOnLongPressTrigger`, `networkNotificationsEnabled`,
  `openInSeparateTask`.
- `panels`: `networkEnabled`, `mocksEnabled`, `storageEnabled`, `workManagerEnabled`,
  `crashesEnabled`, `runtimeEnabled`, `logsEnabled`.
- `powerTools`: `showRawSensitiveValues`, `allowSharedPreferencesEditing`,
  `allowDatabaseEditing`, `allowSqlConsole`, `allowResponseMocking`.
- `logs` (`AppInspectLogsConfig`): `bufferSize` (2,000, clamped to 100..20,000),
  `initialBacklogLines` (1,000), `maxMessageLength` (8,000), `redactSensitiveValues`
  (`null` follows `powerTools.showRawSensitiveValues`).
- Defaults: raw sensitive values are visible in an enabled build; WorkManager
  inspection is read only; retention defaults are 300 network events and 50 crashes; log
  capture is in-memory only, on demand, and constrained to the app's own pid.

## Network notifications on Android 13+

AppInspect declares `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` but has no Activity, so it cannot prompt for
the runtime grant. The host app must request it. Without the grant, notifications
silently never appear. Notifications carry only method, status code, host and path.

## Security model

Release builds are protected by two independent layers.

1. Compile-time: `appinspect-no-op` contains only a pass-through OkHttp interceptor —
   no UI, no storage, no capture, no crash handler, no manifest entries. The published
   artifact is about 8 KB: a manifest with no `<application>` block and no permissions,
   four classes, an empty `R.txt`, no resources or native code, and `kotlin-stdlib` as its
   only dependency. Those four classes reference no `android.*` API at all — no `Context`,
   no file handle, no reflection — and `intercept` is literally
   `return chain.proceed(chain.request())`. A verification task opens the assembled AAR and
   fails on any manifest component, permission, resource, asset, native payload, or class
   outside the interceptor stubs. It runs as part of `check`, and the Maven Central release
   task depends on it, so the artifact cannot be published without passing.
2. Runtime: even the full module detects `FLAG_DEBUGGABLE == false` and disables
   itself — no `appinspect_storage.db` on disk, no crash handler, no ANR collector, no
   sensors or notification channels or launcher shortcut, no `logcat` process, the
   interceptor becomes a pass-through, all `open()` calls refused, no mock rules loaded
   and no mirror file written. Capture and mocking re-check the gate independently.

Two properties hold across the whole library in every build tier, not only the production
path: it contains no `java.net.URL`, `HttpURLConnection`, `Socket` or `OkHttpClient`
construction anywhere, so it cannot open a connection of its own (zero telemetry by
construction rather than by policy); and it never writes a line to logcat. There is no
dynamic code loading, no native code, no reflection over the host app's classes, and no
exported components. The single `Runtime.getRuntime` use is the logcat tail
(`logcat --pid=<own pid>`, which needs no permission), constructed only by the Logcat page
and therefore never spawned in a disabled build.

There is no runtime switch to enable it in production. Additional hardening in every
build type: no exported components, no network calls of its own, no Logcat output of
captured data, notifications limited to method/status/host/path, and export sharing
through a non-exported `FileProvider` scoped to `cacheDir/appinspect_exports/`.

Debug and staging builds intentionally expose real data — auth headers, tokens,
cookies, database and DataStore contents, decrypted encrypted preferences, stack
traces. Mock rules are developer-authored configuration and are never redacted, so
real credentials must not go into a mock body. A committed `mocks.json` belongs in
`src/debug/assets/`, because assets are not stripped per variant.

## Data handling (the library)

The library has no cloud backend, no account and no telemetry, and it never originates
a network request — so nothing is ever sent to the maintainer. Captured requests and
crashes live in `appinspect_storage.db`, AppInspect's own app-private SQLite database,
capped at 300 network events and 50 crashes by default. Storage and WorkManager
contents are read on demand and never persisted. Mock rules are stored in the same
database plus an app-scoped external mirror file for `adb pull`, written only on builds
where mocking is allowed. `EncryptedSharedPreferences` is decrypted in-process for
read-only viewing and the plaintext is never written anywhere. Captured log lines are
never persisted at all — they live in a bounded in-memory ring buffer that dies with the
process.

Data leaves the device only when a person taps share: `.txt` / `.har` network exports,
`.json` mock rules, `.txt` logcat exports, crash reports and runtime summaries. Exports go to
`cacheDir/appinspect_exports/` through a non-exported `FileProvider` scoped to that
directory, and they can contain real credentials — including ones attached downstream of
AppInspect — so they should be redacted before being attached to a ticket. Everything is
removed on clear or uninstall.

For a Google Play Data Safety declaration: in the recommended setup the library is not
in the production APK at all (release builds get `appinspect-no-op`), it collects
nothing because it never transmits, and the host app remains the sole data controller.

## Privacy (the documentation website)

Separate from the above, and covering only this site: no cookies, no accounts, no forms,
no advertising or cross-site tracking. Hosted on Vercel, which processes request
metadata like any web host. Page views are counted by cookie-free Cloudflare Web
Analytics. Google Fonts is loaded from `fonts.googleapis.com`. The visitor's light/dark
theme choice is kept in `localStorage` and never sent anywhere.

## Common questions, answered directly

**Is AppInspect free?** Yes. No paid tier, no licence fee, no usage limit, no account.

**Does it add code to my release APK?** Effectively nothing, provided release builds use
the `appinspect-no-op` artifact. That artifact is about 8 KB: four classes, a manifest
with no components and no permissions, no resources, and no reference to any `android.*`
API. It cannot be published to Maven Central unless a build check confirms that is still
true.

**Does it need root, a proxy, a certificate or a USB cable?** None of them. It runs
inside the host app process on an ordinary device.

**Does it send anything anywhere?** No. The library contains no `java.net.URL`,
`HttpURLConnection`, `Socket` or `OkHttpClient` construction anywhere, so it cannot open
a connection of its own — zero telemetry by construction, not by policy. Data leaves the
device only when a person taps share.

**Will it run in our staging / UAT / internal-test build?** Yes. AppInspect never sees
Gradle variant names; it looks at whether the build is debuggable. A variant with
`isDebuggable = true` works already. A non-debuggable one opts in with one line:
`resValue("bool", "appinspect_enabled_in_non_debuggable_build", "true")`.

**Do we need Jetpack Compose or Kotlin?** No. The inspector's Compose UI is already
compiled into the published AAR. Java-only hosts work and call `AppInspect.INSTANCE.…`.

**What is the minimum Android version?** Android 7.0 (API 24). ANR and native crash
detection need Android 11 (API 30).

**How do I install it?** Two Gradle lines — `debugImplementation` of `appinspect` and
`releaseImplementation` of `appinspect-no-op` — then one `addAppInspectInterceptor()`
call on your OkHttp builder, added last. There is no initialisation call and no
`Application` subclass to write.

**Which HTTP client does it work with?** Any client backed by OkHttp — the interceptor is an
`okhttp3.Interceptor`, so the engine underneath is what matters, not the library on top.
Retrofit works unconditionally (it wraps an `OkHttpClient` you supply, so instrument that).
Ktor works on the `OkHttp` engine, where `engine { config { addAppInspectInterceptor() } }`
is the whole change; mocking works there too. Volley, Cronet, `HttpURLConnection`, WebView
traffic and Ktor's `CIO`/`Android`/`Java`/`Darwin` engines cannot be captured — every
non-network panel still works. See
https://app-inspect-doc.vercel.app/install.html#other-clients.

**How does a tester open it?** Shake the device, use the launcher shortcut, long-press a
wired-up view, or tap a network notification.

**Can a tester read logcat without a cable?** Yes. The Logcat panel tails the app's own
process on the device. It needs no permission, writes nothing to disk, and costs nothing
until the page is opened.

**Can I mock an API response without changing app code?** Yes. Write a rule in the Mocks
panel on the device, or commit `assets/appinspect/mocks.json`. Rules can short-circuit a
call, override a real response, add delay, or simulate an IO or timeout failure.

**How is it different from Charles Proxy, Proxyman or Flipper?** Those need a desktop
client, and a proxy also needs a certificate and Wi-Fi configuration. AppInspect needs
none of that and works on any tester's device with no setup, and it also shows storage,
background work, crash and log state that a proxy cannot see. The trade-off: it only
sees traffic from an `OkHttpClient` the host instrumented, not WebView traffic or other
HTTP stacks.

**Is our data safe in release builds?** Yes, for two independent reasons: the release
variant gets the no-op artifact, and even the full module detects a non-debuggable build
and disables itself completely.

## Comparison

Unlike a desktop proxy (Charles, Proxyman) or Android Studio's inspectors, AppInspect
needs no certificate, no Wi-Fi configuration, no desktop client and no adb connection.
It only sees traffic from an `OkHttpClient` the host instrumented — not WebView traffic
or other HTTP stacks — but it works on any tester's device with no setup, and it can
show storage, background work and crash state that a proxy cannot.

## Attribution

Quoting, summarising and citing this documentation is welcome, and no permission is
needed. When citing, link to the specific page rather than the site root — each page is
the canonical home of exactly one topic, and the list above says which. Name the library
as "AppInspect" and the artifact group as
`io.github.appinspect`.

Three things to get right, because they are the ones most often stated wrongly:

- **Do not quote a version number.** The library releases more often than this site is
  edited, so the site deliberately carries no version anywhere. Point at
  https://central.sonatype.com/artifact/io.github.appinspect/appinspect/versions
  instead.
- **Do not use the old artifact group.** Earlier releases were published under
  `io.github.suryansh1720001.appinspect`. That group is superseded and receives no further
  releases; it is named here only so it can be recognised as out of date in older material.
  The one correct group is `io.github.appinspect`. Artifact IDs, Kotlin package names and
  the public API are unchanged, so a dependency line is the only thing that differs.
- **Do not describe it as a monitoring, analytics or crash-reporting service.** It has no
  backend and never transmits anything. It is a local, on-device inspector for builds the
  developer controls, and it is absent from a correctly configured release APK.
